strengths: The paper presents an intuitive and computationally lightweight method for organizing SAE features across layers using coactivation graphs, addressing a relevant mechanistic-interpretability question.

Targeted interventions produce striking, interpretable behavioral changes. In particular, the reported country, relation, and composite steering results provide useful evidence that the selected feature sets carry behaviorally relevant information.
The use of a distinct prompt template for steering offers some evidence of context transfer, while replication on Gemma 2 9B suggests that the observations are not unique to the 2B checkpoint.

The paper is clearly written and visually communicates the pipeline, extracted components, intervention examples, and layer distributions. The distinction between early country components and later relation components is an interesting hypothesis for further study.
The evaluation covers all combinations of ten countries and three relations rather than relying solely on a few qualitative demonstrations.
weaknesses: The intervention procedure is not specified sufficiently for reproduction. The manuscript does not give an operational equation for ablation or amplification, identify precisely where and at which token positions SAE activations are modified, explain how modified features are decoded into the residual stream, or describe generation settings and the criterion used to judge an answer successful. Reporting only tuned strength values in the appendix does not resolve this omission.

Steering strengths are selected to maximize success on the same prompts used to report success, including a further search around the individually optimized strengths for composite steering. There is no held-out development/test split, so the 90–96% headline rates are optimistically selected estimates rather than clean generalization results.

Component discovery is partly outcome-guided: components are prioritized through post-ablation KL divergence and then intersected across the same small set of countries and relations. Testing a new wording with the same entities and facts is limited evidence of context consistency, and does not establish generalization to unseen entities, relations, paraphrase families, languages, or domains.

Essential causal controls are absent. The study does not compare against size-, layer-, activation-, or density-matched random feature sets; individual high-activation features; shuffled components; non-connected feature sets; or simpler activation-steering baselines. Consequently, the evidence shows that selected features can steer outputs, but not that graph connectivity discovers uniquely meaningful modules or materially improves over simpler selection procedures.

The graph edges are correlations across token positions within a single short prompt, not causal interactions or information-flow edges. Highly correlated features can merely respond to the same tokens. Weakly connected components of this graph therefore do not by themselves justify the strong claims of network modules, organization of knowledge, or compositional causal structure.

The apparent compositionality result could follow from simultaneous additive steering by two independently selected feature sets. There is no comparison against predictions from the individual interventions, no interaction analysis, and no test of systematic composition beyond a narrow country-by-relation grid.

The layer-organization claims are descriptive and weakly supported. They rely on only three relation types, provide no uncertainty or statistical tests, and fit unspecified regressions to highly skewed KL values. Moreover, a component's earliest layer is partly determined by graph construction, top-k selection, correlation thresholds, and SAE properties; sensitivity analyses for k, correlation threshold, density threshold, and SAE reconstruction quality are missing.

Semantic coherence is assessed mainly through model-generated Neuronpedia descriptions and selected examples, without blinded human annotation or a quantitative coherence metric. The acknowledged Spain failure further cautions against treating these labels as validated component semantics.

The two evaluated models belong to one model family and rely on the same SAE ecosystem. No comparison with prior circuit-discovery methods is given for faithfulness, computational cost, or steering quality, despite efficiency being a stated contribution.

No code or complete artifact-release statement is provided, and several implementation details, component identities, prompt templates, target-answer rules, and per-example predictions are absent. Thus the present manuscript is not adequately reproducible. These concerns require important but feasible experimental and reporting revisions, supporting resubmission rather than Findings acceptance. strengths: The manuscript presents an intuitive, computationally lightweight pipeline for grouping cross-layer SAE features and applies it to a concrete mechanistic-interpretability question. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/861ba55c21e2473298a2d787b0776bd9/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The ablation and amplification results are striking at face value: country, relation, and combined interventions frequently elicit the intended counterfactual answer.
Testing two model sizes and using a second prompt template provide some evidence that the observations are not confined to one checkpoint or the exact discovery prompt.
The paper is clearly written and situated reasonably well relative to work on SAEs, factual recall, and circuit discovery.
weaknesses: The central causal interpretation is overstated. Correlation of feature activations across token positions does not identify information flow or computational edges; the resulting weakly connected components are therefore coactivation clusters, not demonstrated circuits or modules. Off-manifold amplification shows that a feature set can steer an output, but not that the model naturally uses it as a composable semantic module.

The intervention methodology is insufficiently specified for reproduction. The paper does not give the precise ablation and amplification equations, where and how SAE activations are replaced, how reconstruction error is handled, how the reported steering coefficients are applied, or sufficiently detailed decoding and success-scoring procedures. No implementation or artifact release is identified.

The reported success rates are optimistically biased: steering strengths are selected to maximize success on what appears to be the same complete prompt set used for evaluation. There is no held-out development/test split, cross-validation, or independently fixed hyperparameter protocol.

Component discovery and evaluation involve substantial selection circularity. Components are prioritized by their output effect and interpreted through feature descriptions and post-intervention outputs, after which their causal significance is assessed using closely related tasks. The procedure for matching components across prompts and taking intersections is also underspecified.

Essential controls are absent. The study does not compare against size- and layer-matched random feature sets, activation-matched features, individual SAE features, simpler steering baselines, or components obtained under shuffled correlations. Consequently, it is unclear whether graph connectivity contributes beyond selecting causally potent SAE features.

The empirical scope is narrow: ten countries, three highly formulaic relations, English prompts, and two sizes from one model family using the same SAE ecosystem. Changing only the prompt template is weak evidence for context consistency or general semantic compositionality.

The layer-organization claims lack quantitative support. Figures show regressions, but slopes, uncertainty, significance tests, robustness to thresholds, and controls for component size or layer-dependent intervention sensitivity are not reported. Claims that concrete entities emerge early and abstract relations emerge late therefore remain exploratory.

Several evaluation details are ambiguous, including what counts as a successful answer, whether generation is deterministic, how aliases or multiple valid languages/currencies are treated, and whether the tabled likelihoods are probabilities expressed as percentages. No uncertainty estimates are given.

Overall, the idea is promising but the current evidence does not support a sound and reproducible Findings contribution. A next-cycle revision could become viable by fully specifying the interventions, separating tuning from evaluation, adding matched controls and statistical analyses, and substantially broadening the tasks and robustness tests.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, computationally lightweight pipeline for organizing SAE features across layers using coactivation graphs. The resulting components are intuitively interpretable and relevant to mechanistic interpretability.

Targeted interventions produce striking behavioral changes: country, relation, and composite steering achieve high reported success rates, and composite interventions provide especially interesting evidence that distinct signals can be combined.
Using a prompt template different from the component-discovery template is a useful initial test of context robustness.
The main phenomena are reproduced on Gemma 2 2B and 9B, reducing concern that the results are peculiar to one model size.
The paper is clearly written, well motivated, and visually communicates the pipeline and qualitative results effectively. The topic is directly relevant to NLP interpretability and model control.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not properly held out. Steering coefficients are explicitly selected to maximize success rates, apparently on the same prompt sets used for the reported results. Without a development/test separation, the headline 90–97% rates may substantially overestimate generalization.

Critical intervention details are missing. The paper does not mathematically specify how SAE features are ablated or amplified, how modified SAE activations are mapped back into the residual stream, where hooks are applied, or how reconstruction error is handled. The success criterion, decoding procedure, and treatment of aliases or multi-token answers are also unspecified. No code or complete prompt/component release is identified, preventing adequate reproducibility.

There are no matched controls or competitive baselines—for example, random components matched for size, activation magnitude or layer, individual high-activation features, non-graph feature sets, or established activation-steering methods. Consequently, the experiments show that selected feature interventions can steer outputs, but do not establish that coactivation graphs are necessary or superior.

Component selection is partly post hoc and insufficiently formalized. Roughly 70 components are extracted per prompt, high-impact components are inspected for semantic meaning, and cross-context intersections are then labeled as country or relation components. Quantitative overlap results across all countries and relations, annotation criteria, and controls against selection bias are absent; the paper itself notes that some components lack the claimed semantic descriptions.

Pearson correlations are estimated across the token positions of a single short prompt, making them potentially unstable. There is no null analysis, uncertainty estimate, or sensitivity study for top-k selection, the 0.9 correlation threshold, the density cutoff, or prompt/example choice. Moreover, edge direction and weights do not affect the weakly connected-component extraction.

The evidence for modular organization is narrower than the claims imply. Successful manipulation demonstrates causal influence on outputs, but does not by itself show that the components store knowledge as independent semantic modules; amplification may inject lexical or categorical signals, and component ablation often redirects probability to unrelated countries rather than selectively removing one fact.

The layer-wise conclusions are descriptive and potentially confounded by layer-specific SAE properties and the graph-construction procedure. Regression coefficients, uncertainty, significance tests, cross-prompt consistency, and comparable results for the 9B model are not reported.

External validity is limited to one model family, one SAE family, closely related factual-QA templates, three relations, and ten countries. The second model is a scale replication rather than an independent architecture or domain test. Overall, the core phenomenon is promising, but unresolved evaluation and reproducibility issues prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper presents an interesting, lightweight method for grouping cross-layer SAE features through coactivation and applying the resulting groups to relational knowledge tasks.

Ablation and amplification experiments provide genuine intervention-based evidence that selected feature groups influence model outputs; the compound country-relation and word-language interventions are especially suggestive.
The comparison with the most causally influential single feature supports the value of distributed feature groups in the country-facts setting.

The experiments cover factual and lexical relations, and the country-facts result is partially replicated on Gemma 2 9B. Prompts, task items, accepted answers, and many output distributions are documented.
weaknesses: Component discovery and evaluation are substantially circular. Components are manually selected according to their ablation effects and desired compositional changes; for two tasks, multiple 'seemingly relevant' components are manually unioned. Steering strengths are then chosen to maximize success rates, apparently on the same combinations reported as evaluation. A held-out selection/tuning/evaluation protocol is needed before the headline success rates can support the claims.

The graph construction does not establish computational modules or information flow. Edges are correlations between feature activations across token positions in a single short prompt; shared token-position patterns can induce high adjacent-layer correlation without a causal connection. Weakly connected components of this graph therefore do not by themselves justify the claimed modular organization. Matched random, activation-, layer-, and size-controlled components and causal edge/path tests are missing.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript does not precisely specify how SAE features are amplified or what alpha means, provides no code or complete executable component-selection procedure, and relies on manual judgments. Appendix G is internally inconsistent: the stated search grid and neighborhood cannot produce the reported composite alpha_c'=0.055 for verb transformation.

The evaluation labels were refined after inspecting errors and are unusually permissive, sometimes accepting syntactically or semantically questionable answers such as French 'grand' for 'good,' German 'Flucht' for 'run,' and Spanish 'eres' for 'you.' This post hoc labeling can inflate success rates. There are also no confidence intervals, uncertainty estimates, or robustness analyses despite small and non-independent task sets.

Baseline and ablation coverage is too limited. The single-feature comparison is reported only for country facts, with no matched-size random components, top-activated-feature groups, non-connected groups, or sensitivity analyses for top-k, correlation threshold, density threshold, component size, and SAE reconstruction error. These controls are necessary to show that coactivation connectivity, rather than selecting many high-impact features, drives the results.

The broad conclusions are not supported by the narrow evidence: most results use one 2B model, three small hand-built tasks on which the model is preselected for 100% accuracy, and a second model only on the easiest country task. Composite steering is only 22% for verb transformations, and ablating those components reduces unrelated-task accuracy to 64–73%, contradicting a general claim of specific semantic modules.

The layerwise interpretation is descriptive and potentially confounded by layer-dependent SAE quality, activation scale, component size, and the selection procedure. No statistical tests or controls establish that concepts generally emerge early while abstract relations emerge late.

Overall, the intervention results are promising, but resolving the circular experimental design, specifying the method fully, adding controls and held-out evaluation, and narrowing or substantiating the modularity claims require an important revision before the work meets Findings-level soundness and reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant mechanistic-interpretability question and proposes an intuitively simple pipeline for grouping cross-layer SAE features using coactivation. The assessment is based on the complete manuscript, including appendices and figures: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/4f66d360f2d54db8b6220780ce76e822/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

Interventions provide genuine evidence that the selected feature sets can influence next-token predictions. The counterfactual and composite-steering experiments are particularly useful demonstrations, and the country-fact results are partially replicated on Gemma 2 9B.

The paper reports more than favorable examples: it gives aggregate success rates, a single-feature comparison, cross-task ablations, detailed task specifications, and several conspicuous failures, including weak verb-transformation and transcoder results.

The presentation is generally clear, and the distinction between concept and relation components, together with their differing layer distributions, is an interesting hypothesis for future investigation.
weaknesses: The decisive problem is circular evaluation. Components are manually selected by inspecting feature descriptions and intervention outputs; for two task families, multiple components are combined based on being “seemingly relevant.” Steering strengths are then chosen to maximize the reported success rates, apparently on the same examples. Even the accepted-answer lists were refined after inspecting outputs initially counted as errors. With no held-out selection, validation, and test split, the reported accuracies do not establish that the method reliably discovers semantic modules rather than fitting the evaluated cases.

The method is not specified reproducibly enough. The manuscript does not provide an operational definition of SAE-feature ablation or amplification, explain how reconstruction errors are handled, or fully specify the manual component-selection heuristics. No code or immutable artifact is identified. Consequently, an independent researcher could construct the graph but could not reliably reproduce the central interventions or component choices.

The evidence does not isolate the benefit of coactivation graphs. The only principal baseline uses one maximally causal feature. Missing controls include size-matched random or top-activated feature sets, components formed without correlation edges, alternative thresholds, density-matched features, and automated circuit-discovery baselines. Thus, better performance than one feature does not show that the discovered graph topology identifies a meaningful module.

Edges are based on Pearson correlations across token positions within a single short prompt, often involving sparse activations and few observations. There is no null model, significance analysis, robustness study, or correction for correlations induced by token position and shared sparsity. Weak connectivity under arbitrary thresholds is then treated as a functional component, although correlation between adjacent-layer SAE features does not establish information flow or a computational circuit.

The scope is very small and selectively favorable: three small task families are retained because Gemma already attains 100% accuracy, while unsuccessful tasks are excluded. Most evidence comes from one 2B model; the 9B extension covers only country facts. Results generalize poorly within the retained suite—for example, composite verb-transformation steering averages 22%, with essentially zero success for several relations—and transcoder steering reaches only 27%.

Semantic specificity is overstated. Ablating verb-transformation components reduces accuracy on every task to roughly 64–73%, indicating broad disruption. Permissive, post-hoc answer sets and counting tokens that may merely begin an answer further weaken the interpretation of steering success. No confidence intervals, repeated runs, or statistical tests are reported.

The claim that early-layer concept components and late-layer relation components reveal a hierarchical organization is exploratory rather than established. Component selection, SAE feature availability, component size, and the intervention procedure can all confound layer location; the plotted regressions lack uncertainty or hypothesis tests. Overall, the work contains a promising idea, but the current evidence does not adequately support the headline claim of discovering causal semantic modules. A resubmission needs a fully specified automatic selection procedure, preregistered or held-out evaluation, stronger controls and robustness analyses, and broader model/task validation.

strengths: The paper presents a simple and potentially useful idea: constructing cross-layer graphs from SAE-feature coactivation and extracting sparse connected components associated with concepts and relations.

The intervention results provide meaningful causal evidence beyond feature-description inspection. Ablating and amplifying components often changes predictions in semantically predictable ways, with particularly strong results for country facts and reasonably strong results for translation.

Joint concept–relation interventions are an appealing contribution. Results such as composing a target country with a target relation support a limited but interesting form of modular compositionality.

The authors include several useful checks: a single-feature baseline, cross-task ablations, layerwise analyses, alternate prompt templates, detailed per-concept results, and replication of the strongest country-fact result on Gemma 2 9B.
The paper is clearly written, visually polished, relevant to mechanistic interpretability in NLP, and unusually candid about unsuccessful tasks and the weaker verb-transformation results.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not cleanly separated from component and hyperparameter selection. Components are manually chosen using semantic descriptions and behavioral effects, while steering strengths are selected to maximize the reported success rates. No held-out validation/test split is described. Consequently, changing the prompt template does not establish genuine out-of-sample generalization, and the reported rates may substantially overestimate reliability.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a Findings recommendation in the current form. The paper does not precisely define the amplification intervention, provides no complete algorithm for the manual union/selection of “seemingly relevant” components, and does not identify a released implementation or fixed component lists. Independent researchers could not reconstruct the principal experiments from the manuscript alone.

The evidence is narrow and selectively conditioned on tasks where the model already achieves 100% accuracy. The main study covers only 10 countries, 11 words, and 8 verbs in one model; attempted unsuccessful domains are excluded, and the 9B replication covers only the easiest country task. Claims about general relational knowledge or a broadly modular organization therefore exceed the demonstrated scope.

Important controls are missing. The component method is compared only with the single most causal feature on one task, not with matched-size random components, top-k causal features without graph structure, activation-magnitude-matched features, or established steering/circuit baselines. Thus, the results do not isolate whether coactivation connectivity provides value beyond aggregating many behaviorally selected features.

The construction choices—top five features, correlation threshold 0.9, density threshold 0.01, and correlations computed over the few tokens of a single templated prompt—receive no sensitivity or null analysis. With such short repeated templates, high correlations and connected components can arise from shared token-position patterns rather than semantic coordination.

Several central characterizations are qualitative or overstated. Context consistency is illustrated rather than systematically quantified; correlation edges do not establish information flow between layers; and the very low composite performance on verb transformations (0.22 overall, including zeros for several relations) substantially limits the claimed compositionality.

The answer sets were refined after inspecting nominal errors and include permissive semantic or syntactic alternatives. Without a preregistered evaluation rule, independent annotation, or full-output evaluation, this post-hoc process can inflate steering success.

Overall, the core proof of concept is promising, but held-out evaluation, a fully specified intervention and component-selection procedure, stronger controls, and robustness analyses are needed before the contribution is sufficiently sound and reproducible for Findings.
